items.text: Loss or corruption of specification content
Two people edit one document and the reconciliation silently drops an item, duplicates an id, or leaves a reference pointing at something that no longer exists.
items.notes: A line-based merge of a formatted JSON array produces exactly this and the result looks plausible in review, which is why the merge is item-id-keyed and textual merging of a register is refused outright.

items.text: An edit written against a version of a document that has since moved overwrites another person's change without either of them being told.
items.notes: Version tags seen on read are replayed on write; the server refuses the stale write rather than the client detecting it.

items.text: A working copy holding unpublished edits is removed while reclaiming idle disk, and the work exists in no git object.
A user edits the hosted demo, believes the result was saved, and loses the work on reload.
items.notes: The sandbox states that nothing is saved and offers the document as a download; the transport refuses writes as a backstop.

items.text: Evidence that is not what it appears to be
A test that never executed is reported as passing, so a requirement appears verified when nothing verified it.
items.notes: A link resolving to no result is "not run", which is a distinct state from failed and from passed. This register exists largely to make that distinction load-bearing: it is the claim the whole export rests on.

items.text: A change enters the repository without validation or governance, so the published evidence is internally inconsistent.
items.notes: Governance runs server-side because the client is not trusted. For someone who never runs the test suite, this gate is the only thing enforcing the rule.

items.text: Renaming a human label breaks a trace link, and the requirement, test or design silently stops being connected to what it was connected to.
items.notes: Every reference targets a generated immutable id; codes are labels nothing resolves by. An unresolved reference is reported rather than hidden.

items.text: The design or architecture drifts from the code it claims to describe, so a reviewer reads a description of software that no longer exists.
items.notes: Detected rather than prevented: the pre-push check names each changed file with the design section claiming it. It warns, because only the author can say whether the design moved.

items.text: A crafted path escapes the allowlisted project directory, letting a request read or write application source in the repository the server can push to.
items.notes: Two independent defences: the path grammar refuses traversal outright, and sparse-checkout means the working tree cannot contain application source for a path bug to reach.

items.text: A user whose role does not permit editing changes the specification anyway.
items.notes: The editor's read-only rendering is a courtesy; the refusal is server-side and does not depend on what the client displayed.

items.text: A commit published through the server is attributed to the machine credential rather than to the person who made it, so the change history misstates who changed the specification.
The git repository holding the specification is lost, or its history is rewritten, and the evidence chain goes with it.
items.justification: Controlled outside SpecPad: the repository is the customer's, and its durability, backup and branch protection belong to their hosting and quality system. SpecPad never force-pushes and never rewrites history, which is the whole of its contribution.
